Quotations for cathode import premiums have declined during the last fortnight. They now fall into the range of $40-$70/t, down from the $70-$80/t range we reported in our last publication. The premium for SXEW material is currently being quoted at $40/t, down from prior range of $40-$55/t. Market activity has been characterised as quiet and this not surprising considering the high stock levels. In late July, prices experienced a large decline after market sentiment turned more negative following news that Spain would likely need a more substantial bail-out than previously thought. The SHFE spot price did not decline quite as far as the exchange-traded prices, thanks to the high level of inventory, as well as sluggish demand. Although the SHFE/LME arbitrage has become more favourable to imports once again, we have not heard any reports that cathode demand is accelerating. Confirmation that domestic market demand has been rather lacklustre is that refined copper production, as reported by the NBS in July, amounted to 483,000 tonnes, a decline of 6.8% compared to the 518,000 tonnes of output reported in June. In fact, the latest macroeconomic data signal that the Chinese economy is not likely to gather momentum until perhaps Q4. Industrial production in July rose by 9.2% y-o-y, the slowest pace since May 2009, and below the Q2 growth rate of 9.5%. Whilst fixed ass

et investment on a year-to-date basis is running 20.9% higher than during the first seven months of 2011, this growth rate represents a continuation of the declining trend in this indicator which has been in place since November 2011.  That said, spending on investment during 2012 has been reportedly running behind schedule, so there may be room for some acceleration in capital spending later this year, which could support demand going into Q1 2013. Both the official and HSBC/Markit PMIs showed that although manufacturing output levels appear to have stabilised, there is still little very little momentum being generated by the export sector.  Inflation in July was reported at 1.8%, down from the June rate of 2.2%. With inflation running below the central bank’s target, there is certainly room for the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) to implement further monetary easing.  However, the PBOC seems to be on hold, evaluating the effects of the rate cut which it enacted two months ago, the effects of which have not worked through the economy as yet. 

Not content to wait for new official action, the private sector has stepped in with an idea of its own.  Beginning August 10<sup>th</sup> , the China Household Electrical Appliances Association announced that producers and retailers will subsidise purchases of kitchen appliances, including microwave ovens, electric cookers, electric fans and extraction fans, by as much as 10% of the sales price. The scheme’s effectiveness will be reviewed in 40 days. 

# Cathode export tax removed 

Since, 1<sup>st</sup> February 2009, the country’s seven largest copper smelters (Anhui Tongling Nonferrous, Jiangxi Copper, Hubei Daye Nonferrous, Yunnan Copper, Gansu Jinchuan Group Co., Ltd, Shandong

Yanggu Xiangguang Copper, Gansu Baiyin Ibis Copper) have been able to import copper concentrate on a tolling basis. The smelters did not have to pay the 17% VAT on the imported metal, but they were required to pay the 3% VAT when the metal was exported.  Our Beijing analysts have confirmed that, as of July 1<sup>st</sup> , this 3% export tax has been lifted.  Now, the smelters have to pay 17% VAT on the valueadded part of the cathode export, which essentially amounts to the TC/RC. 

To get a sense of what this means for the smelters, if we assume no price difference between the LME and SHFE, and a TC/RC cost of RMB2000 (or US$300/t), the VAT to be paid under the new policy amounts to $43.60/t. Prior to this, the VAT cost was approximately $270/t. As a result, the smelters will now receive a tax break of about $226/t, making it much more favourable for them to export cathode whenever the LME price is above that on the SHFE. 

The question is, will this new policy result in additional cathode exports? News reports indicate that some smelters intend to export more cathode in the near-term. However, as the chart below indicates, this i

As illustrated above, following the crash in 2008, it was rather lucrative for Chinese smelters to export cathode. The policy enacted in February 2009 was clearly put into place to discourage this speculative trading. Instead, it incentivized a build-up in copper stocks in China, at a time when prices were very low. This not only helped the global copper market to recover, but it also provided the Chinese with a buffer of inventory that could be drawn from when a tighter physical market emerged in the future. The chart clearly indicates that smelters do not have much of an incentive to export cathode at the moment. Even though the arbitrage between the SHFE and LME prices has now turned positive, it is nowhere near the $470/t that Macquarie has quoted as sufficient to encourage this type of activity. # First standards published for CCA bus bars On July 1st , the new standards published by the State Energy Bureau for the use of copper clad aluminium CCA bus bars in power transforming and transmitting facilities went into effect. CCA bus bars have a copper volume of between 18% and 22% - the balance is aluminium. Although this could reduce the consumption of © 2012 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 4 **August 2012** www.crugroup.com copper in this application, the effect will not be immediate. Not only will it take time for the market to adopt this new product, but the recycling of this compound material may be more difficult, thereby discouraging its use. According to the China Nonferrous Industry Association, China produced 353,583 tonnes of copper bar in 2010.
